item.title: Staff at the US center for AI safety are reporting to the White House
Show HN: Airlock – Policy-as-code for fleets of AI coding agents
item.description:
My name is Matt and I am building Airlock. Airlock is going to be an open standard on managing autonomous fleets of engineering agents. I am seeking constructive feedback on the direction of this project and also asking what are your major pain points with managing AI use at larger businesses. Right now I am running my own company using this framework with a total of 23 workflows across four large scale projects.

Airlock is still really early, only 3-4 weeks old.

Airlock's configuration standard is aimed to be open source and I will also open source the backplane once I gain a bit more confidence in what I have built here and it is a bit more ready for public scrutiny. Today the schema itself and the reusable GitHub actions are publicly available. I will selfishly figure out how to monetize this at some point but my desired customer is going to be larger enterprises. Airlock kind of does a lot of things but if I had to sum it up in several bullet points it would be:

1) Allows for the configuration of agent behaviors and life cycles under version control. Each agent run proves who it is with GitHub’s OIDC token, and Airlock trades that for a GitHub token that lasts one hour and can only touch the repos and permissions listed in that agent’s role file.

2) Allows for configuring levels of autonomy starting with a repository's base autonomy level with stricter overrides down to individual files within a code base. (e.g. you trust agents for most of the repo but perhaps you want extra gating around the 'billing' or 'auth' modules).

3) Supports a standard autonomy scale. At level 4 agents are leading a project's direction while at level 1 they are dependent on humans to lead the direction of a project.

4) Provides an out-of-the-box OTEL collector that stores a subset of agent actions you would care about in the event of an audit. I’m exploring storing agent prompts and user prompts so that only the customer can decrypt them, and haven’t decided how.

5) Comes with a shadow mode that allows you to run Airlock and observe how it would behave in your org without turning it on.

To try it you just need to install the GitHub App, create a policy repository and run on GitHub hosted runners. I personally use self-hosted runners on EC2 spot instances. Visit https://airlock.lunareng.com/docs/quickstart to get started.

I have been really passionate lately about exploring how businesses of the [near] future will effectively manage autonomous development using agents at scale. I want to help answer the question of how can the business better manage AI spend, prioritization of token usage, auditability of agent actions and compliance with various governance, risk and compliance frameworks.

I am coming from the perspective of being an engineer for 15+ years but I have somehow managed to also develop a good understanding of how larger businesses operate. My vision of the future looks like a world where engineers don't use agent harnesses directly from their computer [for coding]. Instead engineering teams are managing a larger backlog of work that is automatically picked up by these agents. Engineering will instead be less about writing code and more about effectively deploying technology to solve business problems.

Thanks for taking a look and I look forward to meeting you in the comments.

References: https://github.com/lunareng/airlock-actions https://airlock.lunareng.com/schema/role.schema.json https://airlock.lunareng.com/schema/autonomy.schema.json https://airlock.lunareng.com/schema/config.schema.json https://www.anthropic.com/institute/measuring-pace-of-ai-dev... https://felixrieseberg.com/how-to-be-more-ambitious-a-tutori...

Show HN: My first project, an AI-powered financial news analyzer
item.description:
I'm 17, and I started NotBot a few months ago to see whether I could turn an idea into a working project. My main interest is economics, not becoming a programmer, but I enjoy experimenting with code.

A few months ago, I had the idea of creating a program that would analyze the most recent news about a specific stock and calculate a weighted average of their polarity to create a sort of sentiment indicator.

While researching, I found a YouTube video about creating a simple GitHub repository that did, in a simplified and imprecise way, what I had in mind. At first glance, I realized it was a very simple program: feedparser retrieved news from Google News, beautifulsoup4 extracted the content, the sentiment was analyzed with FinBERT, running through Transformers and PyTorch.

From there, I started modifying it with the free versions of Gemini. I had to solve a lot of problems, for example fixing the extraction of articles from Google News, I managed to solve it with a new library (googlenewsdecoder).

Then I had to replace FinBERT, because it classified sentiment based on the context of the words but didn't take into account the actual impact of the event using external sources.

I experimented with an LLM that allowed me to specify the evaluation criteria more precisely through a prompt. I found a free one with rather strict TPM and RPM limits (it was called openai/gpt-oss-120b).

I also created two coefficients: one that adjusted the reliability of the news based on its source, and another that adjusted its impact based on how recent it was (all selected news articles had been published within the last 24 hours). Each article was divided into title, description, and content, and each of these three sections had a different weight based on predefined values (title 35%, description 25%, and text 40%). If the content had fewer than 100 characters, the text was not assigned any weight, and the title accounted for 60% while the description accounted for 40%.

After these modifications, I took a break of about a month because of school commitments, during which I discovered Codex (OpenAI's agent).

I changed the main LLM and implemented Gemini (3.1 Flash-Lite) because the TPM limits of the LLM I was using were too restrictive.

Even though I started using Gemini, I didn't discard Groq. In fact, I used it as a fallback in case Gemini returned some kind of error.

Another important modification was the addition of asynchronous article downloading through aiohttp and the processing of multiple articles simultaneously through asyncio. Later, I decided to start using Groq again for article analysis. In fact, I had both LLMs analyze the longer articles and then calculated the average of their two polarity scores.

The first was Finnhub, which allowed me to search for many more news articles about a specific stock (by entering its name and ticker).

At that point, I had to split up the code because the script had become very long.

The last modification I made concerned news selection: I implemented a filter that prevented similar news articles from being selected, to avoid excessively distorting the polarity in an incorrect way.

First of all, I'd like to know, from an expert, how well the project is built from a structural point of view and how it could be improved. For future projects, what parameters should I take into consideration to understand whether a project is well built?

Secondly, I'd like to know how I can determine whether a program like this can actually work, or at least how it could be useful (even with some modifications).

The third and final point is: which aspects of the pipeline might require more attention or could be optimized? Does it make sense to continue working on the project (also with the idea of turning it into a product), or am I approaching a structural limit?
